/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.headline: UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.excerpt: Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers. Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand. If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand. The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteries can do the same job. Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need to pay renewable generators to switch off. However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years.
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.trail: V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand

/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.headline: Policy U-turn could stall Britain’s take-up of electric vehicles
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.excerpt: Electric cars make people happy. More than nine in 10 EV drivers – 94% in a recent poll – are saving money, and a similar number would stick with electric for their next purchase, and recommend them to family and friends. Sales are soaring: more than half of the new cars sold in the UK last month were electric, if hybrids are taken into account, and about 28% of new car sales overall were electric only. This is hardly surprising, given that soaring petrol and diesel costs have pushed up the price of a full tank to about £120. EV drivers are paying about 2.4p a mile. Why then is the government considering a major U-turn on electric vehicle policy that, if followed through, could stall the take-up of EVs, help to close off a route to lower living costs, and dent the UK’s ability to meet its carbon targets? Andy Burnham, the prime minister, wrote in the Guardian this week that he would push ahead with the target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Despite the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield this week, sources in government also hinted to the Guardian that another large project, the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, was less likely to be greenlighted. However, analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank, seen by the Guardian, shows that the looming decision on the future of electric vehicles could also have a major impact on net zero and carbon budgets, though it has received far less attention.
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.trail: The 2030 target for 80% of new cars to have zero emissions could be cut to as low as half

/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.headline: Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.excerpt: Elon Musk has revealed Tesla’s latest model, which he claims will be the world’s first flying car, using technology from his aerospace company SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at the SpaceX rocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters. A video of the event shows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters to flip, fly and land. Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models and then accelerate to 60mph in record time. “Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event. Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.” “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”. In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles.
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.trail: The Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and land

/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.headline: Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spaces
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.excerpt: It has no rear window, will not fit into a UK parking space and – starting at £130,000 – ($172,000) is aimed squarely at rich tech industry buyers driving the wide open roads of America. Jaguar’s electric car, the Type 01, was launched in New York on Tuesday night and marks the culmination of a two-year rebrand that has been one of the most scrutinised in automotive history. Bosses hope the vehicle will appeal to a younger, richer audience than the manufacturer’s previous “shrinking and ageing” customer base of “men in their 50s”, said Rawdon Glover, 58, Jaguar’s managing director. With an ultra-long bonnet, low roof and muscular design, the Type 01 is a sharp departure from its predecessor, the F-Type. It is also double the F-Type’s starting price of about £62,000. Buyers are likely to be rich, “urban” and “very design literate, very technology literate”, Glover said. “The person making this purchase will be choosing the car because it’s a bold choice.” A senior JLR executive close to the Type 01 project put it more bluntly: “It’s the type of car that you park up and everybody stops and says: ‘Fucking hell, what have you just turned up in?’” The launch comes at a critical juncture for parent company Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which has grappled with falling sales as cheaper Chinese rivals eat into its UK market share. It is still recovering from a massive cyber-attack last year that cost the economy an estimated £1.9bn.
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.trail: Latest model is launching in New York to target rich US buyers – and is more than 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide

/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.headline: Three-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargers
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.excerpt: Three-quarters of the 20 top-selling plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) in the UK cannot use rapid chargers, research has found, amid concerns that many are essentially “petrol cars pulling round a heavy battery”. The cars, which can run on electric batteries as well as combustion engines, have been promoted by carmakers as a way to cover long distances in a single drive – unlike fully electric cars – while still reducing emissions. But only 26% of the vehicles sold across the top 20 models, which include the Jaecoo 7, the Ford Kuga and Hyundai Tucson, are able to use rapid chargers with powers of 50kW or more, according to analysis by the industry body, ChargeUK. These chargers can quickly top up a car battery – for example at a motorway service station – adding a significant amount of range in 20 to 30 minutes. Cars that cannot use them are limited to much slower charging speeds, meaning drivers wanting to recharge mid-trip may face a wait of several hours. Hybrid owners may instead choose to rely on their petrol engines. Shane Brennan, the chief executive of ChargeUK, said: “A plug-in hybrid electric vehicle that is never plugged in is a costly petrol car pulling round a heavy battery. PHEV drivers unable to charge on the public charging network quickly fall into patterns of being petrol reliant. “Government must not be hoodwinked into promoting the idea that boosting PHEV sales is a meaningful step towards electrification.
/environment/2026/nov/08/labour-cut-ev-t.trail: Only 26% of PHEVs sold across top 20 models can use chargers with power of 50kW or more, analysis finds

/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.headline: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.excerpt: The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans. But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult. The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular. The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous. “These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.” “The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.” Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.trail: Democrats’ sweep could urge Israel’s divided opposition to join forces and remove prime minister closely allied with Trump

/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.headline: Israel’s Herzog yet to decide on who should form government as Eisenkot secures significant backing
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.excerpt: Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first. Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results ‌of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the ‌best shot to form a government. He said he would make a pick on Sunday, and that he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday. A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power. Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.trail: President says he will make a decision on Sunday about who should try to build a government as Netanyahu rival is endorsed by 67 lawmakers

/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.headline: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.excerpt: Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister. The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel. Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing. “In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians. Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud. “The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.trail: Move comes after attorney general blocked Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties

/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.headline: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.excerpt: The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows. There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu. A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel. The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism. The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.
/world/2026/nov/08/gadi-eisenkot-netanya.trail: Survey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in election

/us-news/2026/nov/08/nvidia-jensen-huang.headline: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
/us-news/2026/nov/08/nvidia-jensen-huang.excerpt: US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times. Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources. In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development. White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times. The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security.
/us-news/2026/nov/08/nvidia-jensen-huang.trail: Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China

/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.headline: Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.excerpt: NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners. Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home. Six units have shut permanently since Labour came to power in July 2024. Four others have been closed “temporarily” for so long, up to six years, that childbirth groups fear they will never reopen. Two other birth centres closed because the hospitals where they were based have begun to fall apart and will remain out of action for several years until new facilities are built. Women’s ability to choose where their baby is born is also being increasingly restricted in England and Wales by NHS bodies suspending home birth services for up to 14 months. The wave of closures and suspensions is occurring because of the NHS-wide shortage of midwives, a falling birthrate, the growing complexity of childbirth and a rise in caesarean sections. Campaigners say the loss of local childbirth services is denying women their right to choose and forcing them to travel from their home area to give birth.
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.trail: Twelve midwife-led maternity units have closed in England since 2019 with six closing since Labour came to power in 2024

/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.headline: British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.excerpt: A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment. The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London. Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: “UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.” A humanitarian organisation sent the doctor to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak. The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission. Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.trail: Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital

/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.headline: ‘This is direct’: positive early feedback from pilot community mental health hub in Cumbria
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.excerpt: The night Tamara first walked through the doors of Hope Haven, a new community mental health hub in the heart of Whitehaven, she was afraid. “Terrified, actually,” she says. “Like, my life was falling apart. I didn’t know how to stop it from hurting.” The 22-year-old, who works in children’s transport, had been in and out of therapy and counselling since she was 14, after being abused by an acquaintance as a child. After a lengthy legal process her abuser was sentenced, but the “mental challenge” of dealing with what had happened to her was not over. “I was having a really hard time at home, and my best friend told me that I could go and stay with her for a bit, but I needed to ask for help first, so she dropped me off here at like 11 o’clock at night,” she says. That night was a turning point: Tamara was seen immediately by a member of staff and offered an appointment for the next day. She believes that if she hadn’t been offered help at Hope Haven, she would still be at “rock bottom”. Hope Haven is part of a pilot scheme of six hubs across England. It offers preventive, open-access care 24/7, meaning people do not need a diagnosis or referral to access its services. Its alternative approach reflects concerns that more traditional NHS services have struggled to improve local wellbeing. In its first five months from March to July, about 3,000 people accessed support either digitally or in person.
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.trail: Hope Haven in Whitehaven is one of six trial open-access, 24/7 schemes in England offering preventive care

/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.headline: Welsh health board considers closing urgent primary care centres at three hospitals
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.excerpt: A struggling Welsh health board could close urgent primary care centres at three hospitals, citing funding and recruitment issues, prompting widespread criticism. Betsi Cadwaladr University health board, which serves about a quarter of Wales’s population, said it was consulting on ending urgent primary care centres (UPCCs) at Ysbyty Penrhos Stanley in Holyhead, Ysbyty Alltwen in Tremadog and Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor by April 2027. UPCCs staffed by GPs, advanced nurse practitioners and physiotherapists – similar to urgent treatment centres in England – have been set up across Wales since 2020 to ease pressure on GP practices and emergency departments. Local MPs and MSs from across the political spectrum have written to the board to warn of “dire consequences” – including additional strain on the services they were originally intended to help. The Conservative MS Janet Finch-Saunders, who represents Bangor Conwy Môn, said: “These centres help to relieve pressure on our accident and emergency departments when people are unable to get an appointment with their GP but require immediate care. “It is vital that [the health board] supports these centres to remain open. Without them, existing waiting times could increase, potentially leading to delays in treatment.” Betsi Cadwaladr has been in special measures since 2015 due to concerns over care quality, patient safety and leadership. In June, it was given a “final chance” to improve.
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.trail: Holyhead, Tremadog and Bangor UPCCs may shut as Betsi Cadwaladr University health board struggles with funding

/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.headline: UK government’s obesity plan ‘doomed to fail’, MPs warn
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.excerpt: The UK government’s promise to reverse rising obesity rates in the next decade is “doomed to fail” without a major rethink and a new plan led directly by the prime minister, a cross-party committee of MPs has concluded. The health and social care select committee said in a report that there are no signs the so-called “moonshot ambition on obesity”, set out in the 10-year health plan for England, will achieve anything significant. More than a year after the promise to “end the obesity epidemic” within a decade was made, even the most basic questions – such as how progress will be measured and how a cross-departmental plan would work – remain unanswered, the MPs said. The report said: “While the ambition to ‘end the obesity epidemic’ is a laudable one, we currently have no faith in the government’s commitment to this aim or ability to achieve it and predict that, unless they urgently reassess their approach, they are doomed to fail. “The government will fail to tackle a challenge of this scale unless action is led from the top and delivery of the moonshot is made a clear, personal priority of the prime minister.” It called for the creation of a dedicated cabinet committee on the obesity plan, chaired by the prime minister, to drive action and “to send a message that this government takes obesity seriously”. According to the most recent official statistics, 30% of adults in England are living with obesity, with 66% either overweight or living with obesity.
/society/2026/nov/08/gps-extra-checks-wi.trail: Cross-party committee says ‘moonshot’ vow to end obesity epidemic in a decade will fail without personal leadership from PM

/society/2026/nov/09/few-stroke-survivor.headline: NHS to offer free high-street cholesterol tests in England
/society/2026/nov/09/few-stroke-survivor.excerpt: The NHS in England is to offer free finger-prick blood tests for cholesterol on the high street for the first time under plans to reduce heart disease and stroke deaths by a quarter within the next decade. The seven-minute tests will be available at participating pharmacies as part of a national rollout to spot “ticking timebombs” earlier. People aged 40 to 84 who are not pregnant and have not had a blood test in the past year will be eligible to walk in and get tested. Blood will be taken from a person’s fingertip using a lancet – a small, sharp medical tool used to prick the skin – and analysed immediately. A pharmacist prescriber can then provide lifestyle advice and determine whether any treatment, such as statins, may be needed. Patients will receive a copy of their results by email. They will also be offered a blood pressure check as part of a clinical consultation with a pharmacist prescriber. Details of the scheme – the first of its kind globally – were announced during the European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress in Munich, the world’s largest heart conference. David Webb, the chief pharmaceutical officer for England, said pharmacies could be a vital first line of defence against serious illness. He said: “By making it easier for people to get a quick and convenient cholesterol health check on their local high street, we can spot ticking timebombs earlier, helping people take action, and prevent heart attacks and strokes before they happen.
/society/2026/nov/09/few-stroke-survivor.trail: Checks at pharmacies for people aged 40 to 84 are aimed at identifying those at risk of heart attack or stroke

/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.headline: Hakeem Jeffries supports impeachment of Pete Hegseth: ‘He has got to go’
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.excerpt: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, poised to become majority leader, said on Sunday that he strongly supports impeaching defense secretary Pete Hegseth as a Republican lawmaker prepares to force a House vote. The top Democrat made his position clear during an appearance on ABC’s This Week, declaring himself a “hard yes” on the impeachment resolution targeting Hegseth. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries said. “Pete Hegseth has got to go.” The announcement comes as Kentucky Republican representative Thomas Massie, an outgoing congressman and frequent critic of Donald Trump, moves to revive his impeachment effort against Hegseth. Massie said he plans to reintroduce an impeachment resolution as soon as Monday, potentially setting up a House showdown within days. The measure includes eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of multiple offenses, including violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Asked whether he expects the entire Democratic caucus to support the resolution, Jeffries said members will “have that conversation” Tuesday morning when lawmakers return to Washington for the first time since the midterm elections. “But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution,” Jeffries said.
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.trail: House Democrat is a ‘hard yes’ on impeachment resolution against defense secretary who ‘has abused his power’

/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.headline: Saturday Night Live: Druski hosts and James Talarico cameos, but where’s the post-election comedy?
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.excerpt: Four days after the historic “blue-nami” midterms, Saturday Night Live opens at Democrats’ headquarters, where party leaders Hakeem Jeffries (Kenan Thompson) and Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) celebrate, even as they vow to hold on to power in spite of the wishes of their energized base. Their toast is interrupted by the man responsible for Republicans’ shellacking, Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson). The president, who is “now lame duck”, accepts the results, “which is scarier in a way”. But he’s also resigned to focus on the ballroom, even as he laments having to work with millennial Democrats (this leads him down a long diatribe about the show New Girl). We get quick walk ons by a defeated JD Vance (Jeremy Culhane) and extra-aggro Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost), only for Trump to get a taste of his own medicine when James “Telefreako” Talarico interupts him. Texas’s new senator-elect speaks to one of the big issues of the day: “It’s clear people want something new, they want something different. I’m talking, of course, about SNL’s cold opens. How many of these Trump freezes are they gonna do?” What initially seems like a disappointing rehash of last week’s cold open is somewhat redeemed by Talarico popping in to take the piss out of it (he’s got good timing for a politician). Still, the sheer magnitude of this week’s political shakeup calls for something a little more memorable from what’s supposed to be the nation’s premier satirical institution.
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.trail: SNL booking comedian Druski post-midterms felt misbegotten in low-energy episode failing to capture historic ‘blue-nami’

/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.headline: How CrossFit helped shape the macho fitness culture of Trump’s America
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.excerpt: Comparative machismo is hardly new, but when Donald Trump publicly admired Senator Jon Husted’s backside earlier this month, later telling advisers it made the since-defeated Ohio incumbent more “interesting” to voters, the senator leaned into the compliment, saying it gave him extra motivation to “get down to the gym”. Would that odd exchange have taken place without CrossFit, the fitness empire founded by college dropout and gymnast Greg Glassman in the 1990s that grew to 15,000 gyms across 160 countries before he was drawn into public controversy at the height of #MeToo and the social justice movement in 2020? The question is not directly addressed in The Glass Box, an astonishing new account of Glassman’s spectacular rise and fall and of a fitness movement that encouraged adherents to participate in high-intensity workouts. “Hard Work Pays Off” was the mantra; “Mechanics, Consistency, and then Intensity” was the programming; and “Forging Elite Fitness” was the goal. It was an aesthetic and attitude that even bled into right-wing politics and militarism. But it did not begin that way.

/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.headline: Healthcare, tariffs – but not Trump impeachment: Democrats chart next two years of power
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.excerpt: “Costs, chaos, corruption”: after almost two years spent relentlessly criticizing Donald Trump for failing to address those three, broad political concerns, Democrats won a monumental return to power in Tuesday’s midterm elections that will give them potent new leverage over the president. Now the question becomes: what will they do with it? While party leaders say their exact strategy remains under discussion, all signs point to Democrats embarking on aggressive campaigns of both investigating and lawmaking, with the aim of giving their eventual nominee the ammunition they will need to win the 2028 presidential election. “We are going to make sure that those candidates running for president of the United States aren’t getting asked about plastic-straw bans. Instead, we should be talking about all of the legislation that we pass out of the House, pass out of the Senate, and force to Donald Trump’s desk,” Greg Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told reporters on Wednesday. He envisioned “passing bold legislation that people called for, every single week, off of the floor of the House and the Senate”, pointing to bans on price gouging, Super Pacs and stock trading by lawmakers as priorities. “If [Trump] vetoes it, then that is the platform upon which candidates can run in 2028, and then we can get signed into law in 2029,” Casar said. That election is still two, long and unpredictable years off.

/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.headline: Trump says he asked Dana White, UFC boss, to be his new White House press secretary
/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-tells-60-minu.excerpt: Donald Trump has offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, the president said in a social media post on Saturday. Trump described White, who staged a cage-fighting spectacle at the White House to mark the president’s 80th birthday in June, as “a violent Fighter and Warrior”, credentials unlike any ever used to describe previous press secretaries. Trump added that he asked White, a vocal supporter who campaigned for him in 2024, to bring six UFC fighters with him to serve as press aides. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote. “Dana, please take the job!” It was initially unclear whether the job offer was part of an actual plan, or an attention-grabbing stunt from a president desperate to change the subject from the huge losses suffered by his party in elections this week. There was no immediate response from White, who, some observers noted, might hesitate to leave a lucrative role running the UFC, which has earned him a fortune estimated to be in excess of $600m, for a job in government service that pays $195,000 a year.
